# ARGUMENT QUESTIONS V1 — TEN QUESTIONS OF A NEW SHAPE

*Generated by `scripts/argument-questions.ts` at 2026-08-28 00:06 UTC. Every keyed paragraph below was
read back out of R2 by this run; the text printed under each key is that stored text.*

## What is different about these

Every existing gold question asks **"find the debate about X"**. These ask **"find me the
argument that X"**. The unit of a correct answer is the **paragraph**, not the speech and not
the debate, because the paragraph is what the platform displays.

⚠⚠ **Seven of the ten have their answer in a debate about a different subject**, and that is
the case for an argument graph rather than a decoration on it. The strongest *"nobody will
enforce it"* argument for a short-term lets licensing scheme was made about **Sunday trading
in 1985**; the strongest *"it will just move underground"* argument was made about **wine
auctions in 1944**. No keyword or topic search can reach either of them from the question.

⚠ **Nothing is scored against these.** They are a proposal for Charlie to validate, exactly
as the committees re-key is. A number scored against an unvalidated key is the mistake this
instrument exists to prevent.

## 1. ENFORCEMENT · ⚠ ANSWER IS IN A DEBATE ABOUT A DIFFERENT SUBJECT

**Question:** If we set up a licensing scheme for short-term lets, what's the strongest argument that nobody will actually enforce it?

- **Tag exercised:** `ENFORCEMENT`
- **What the user is asking about:** a licensing scheme for short-term lets
- **Keys:** 3 paragraphs

Nothing in the corpus is about short-term lets licensing. The strongest enforcement arguments were made about social housing regulation in 2016 and about Sunday trading in 1985 and 1994, and every one of them transfers without modification.

- `pwdata-debates:debates2016-01-05d:678#0` — Teresa Pearce, 2016-01-05, 59 words
  <br>**Debate:** *Housing and Planning Bill (Programme) (No. 2) — New Clause 6 — Reducing social housing regulation*

  > Local authorities have the powers but they do not have the resources.

- `pwdata-debates:debates1985-05-20a:230#0` — Mr. Brittan, 1985-05-20, 42 words
  <br>**Debate:** *Shop Hours (Auld Report)*

  > The real reason why they are not enforcing it is that in large parts of the country local people do not want the law enforced.

- `pwdata-debates:debates1994-02-23a:423#0` — Mr. Anderson, 1994-02-23, 112 words
  <br>**Debate:** *New Clause 1 — RESTRICTIONS ON SUNDAY OPENING OF LARGE SHOPS*

  > Therefore, it would have been wasted effort to employ officers who had many other duties to enforce the law when there was a clear signal from the Government —by the Government's inaction—that they were not at all interested in the law being enforced and obeyed.

## 2. UNINTENDED · ⚠ ANSWER IS IN A DEBATE ABOUT A DIFFERENT SUBJECT

**Question:** If we ban selling something outright, what is the argument that it will just move underground?

- **Tag exercised:** `UNINTENDED`
- **What the user is asking about:** banning the sale of a product outright
- **Keys:** 2 paragraphs

The displacement argument in its cleanest form was made in 1944 about the auction of wines and spirits, and in the Lords in the 1980s about a quite different activity. Neither debate is about the product any modern user would be asking about.

- `pwdata-debates:debates1944-03-22a:268#0` — Colonel Llewellin, 1944-03-22, 24 words
  <br>**Debate:** *Oral Answers to Questions — WINES AND SPIRITS (AUCTION SALES)*

  > If we were to prohibit public sales of wines by auction it would obviously drive sales underground.

- `historic-hansard:S5LV0430P0:1761#0` — Lord Somers, 1982-05-17, 137 words
  <br>**Debate:** *Lords: Local Government (Miscellaneous Provisions) Bill*

  > Lord Somers : My Lords, there is a fairly widespread feeling that, if one tries to control what one definitely knows is a wrong activity, there is a great danger that one is merely driving it underground and that it will proceed as usual.

## 4. EVIDENCE_GAP · ⚠ ANSWER IS IN A DEBATE ABOUT A DIFFERENT SUBJECT

**Question:** What's the strongest argument that we are legislating without any evidence the problem is real?

- **Tag exercised:** `EVIDENCE_GAP`
- **What the user is asking about:** a measure whose premise has not been established
- **Keys:** 2 paragraphs

Lord Taylor in 1961 on the Public Health Bill: no evidence tuberculosis is spread by food, therefore reject the clause. The structure — no evidence for the premise, therefore no clause — is the argument, and the subject is incidental.

- `historic-hansard:S5LV0228P0:1989#0` — LORD TAYLOR, 1961-02-21, 116 words
  <br>**Debate:** *Lords: PUBLIC HEALTH BILL [H.L.]*

  > There is no evidence that tuberculosis is spread by food.

- `committees-reports:publication:11130:arc-0009#0` — (no speaker recorded), 2014-10-30, 232 words
  <br>**Debate:** *Report: 11th Report – Draft Child Poverty Act 2010 (Persistent Poverty Target), Draft Marriage Same Sex Couples (Conversion of Civil Partnership), Draft Marriage (Same Sex Couples)*

  > Neither the material laid in support of the Regulations nor the further information now provided seem to us to present hard evidence of direct economic benefit from the changes being made.

## 5. WRONG_VEHICLE

**Question:** What's wrong with a Bill that leaves all the detail to regulations made later by ministers?

- **Tag exercised:** `WRONG_VEHICLE`
- **Keys:** 2 paragraphs

The skeleton-bill objection, stated both by a backbencher in 1983 and by the committee whose job it is. Not cross-subject: the objection is ABOUT legislating, so the debates are too.

- `pwdata-debates:debates1983-04-27a:446#0` — Mr. Cryer, 1983-04-27, 89 words
  <br>**Debate:** *Education (Fees and Awards) Bill*

  > Friend agree that a difficulty under which the House is labouring is that we are dealing with a Bill which is of a sketchy nature which gives virtually unfettered powers to the Secretary of State to produce regulations? Would he further agree that the regulations should be part of the primary legislation, or at least should be produced for the Committee stage? 'The likelihood is that they will not be produced and it will be left to the Secretary of State's powers to produce them subsequently.

- `committees-reports:publication:2750:27198#1` — (no speaker recorded), 2020-09-28, 2372 words
  <br>**Debate:** *Correspondence: Letter from committee Chairs to Michael Gove MP and Jacob Rees-Mogg MP on skeleton bills and skeleton provision (25/09/20)*

  > In a report published in session 1998-99, the DPRRC described skeleton bills as bills which are “little more than a licence to legislate and so give flesh to the ‘skeleton’ embodied in the bill” (29 th Report).

## 6. SCOPE · ⚠ ANSWER IS IN A DEBATE ABOUT A DIFFERENT SUBJECT

**Question:** What is the argument that a new offence is drawn so widely it will catch people who have done nothing wrong?

- **Tag exercised:** `SCOPE`
- **What the user is asking about:** a new offence drawn widely
- **Keys:** 2 paragraphs

The 1927 Trade Disputes Bill names exactly who is wrongly caught and how — law-abiding citizens, without their knowledge. The 1954 Television Bill supplies the other half, an over-broad phrase with an absurd consequence spelled out.

- `historic-hansard:S5LV0068P0:601#0` — (no speaker recorded), 1927-07-12, 235 words
  <br>**Debate:** *Lords: TRADE DISPUTES AND TRADE UNIONS BILL.*

  > The new crimes do not concern criminals so much as law-abiding citizens, who in the ordinary way would desire to obey the law and will now be brought, often without their knowledge and certainly against their will, within the meshes of the Criminal Law and be liable to fine and imprisonment.

- `historic-hansard:S5LV0188P0:2645#0` — LORD SALTOUN, 1954-07-14, 56 words
  <br>**Debate:** *Lords: Prayers — TELEVISION BILL*

  > LORD SALTOUN : I have great sympathy with the noble and learned Earl, but I cannot help feeling that the Amendment is too widely drawn.

## 9. RIGHTS

**Question:** What is the argument that a Bill reverses the presumption of innocence?

- **Tag exercised:** `RIGHTS`
- **Keys:** 2 paragraphs

Two statements of the same objection ninety years apart, one from the 1930s and one tied to an international instrument the Government had just signed.

- `pwdata-debates:debates1934-11-07a:394#0` — Sir W. DAVISON, 1934-11-07, 69 words
  <br>**Debate:** *Orders of the Day — BETTING AND LOTTERIES BILL [Lords] — CLAUSE 20.—(Offences in connection with lotteries.)*

  > It is contrary to the whole of British law that a man should be presumed guilty until the Law Officers of the Crown and the criminal law have proved him to be guilty.

- `pwdata-debates:debates1949-05-03a:433#0` — Mr. Frank Byers, 1949-05-03, 162 words
  <br>**Debate:** *Clause 54.—(PROVISIONS AS TO PROSE- CUTIONS AND AS TO OFFENCES BY CORPORATIONS.)*

  > To what extent are the Government prepared to abide by the Charter of Human Rights? In December the Government signed that Charter, and one of the principles in it was that a man should be presumed innocent until proved guilty.
